newsitem.title: USA: Wholesale sales jump, stocks unchanged in February.
newsitem.headline: Wholesale sales jump, stocks unchanged in February.

text.p: A surge in sales kept wholesalers' inventories flat in February and left them with their lowest supply levels in more than 12 years, the Commerce Department said on Tuesday.
Wholesale sales jumped 2.1 percent in February -- their biggest gain since August 1994 -- to a seasonally adjusted $209.67 billion after a 0.8 percent gain in January, the department said.

Sales were especially brisk for costly and long-lasting durable goods, which rose 2.7 percent in February. They were led by gains in demand for professional equipment, machinery, metals and lumber, the department said.
Sales of quickly used nondurables rose only 1.4 percent in February as declines in chemicals and petroleum partly offset gains in food, paper, clothing and drugs, it said.
The jump in business kept wholesalers from adding to their stocks in February.

Total wholesale inventories were unchanged in February at a seasonally adjusted $260.05 billion. Declines in stocks of automobiles, furniture, petroleum, groceries and drugs offset inventory growth in professional equipment, metals, paper, clothing and farm products, the department said.

With sales up and inventories flat, wholesalers' inventory- to-sales ratio -- a measure of how long it would take to deplete existing stocks at the current sales pace -- dropped to 1.24 months' worth in February, matching a low point last reached in September 1984, the department said. In January, the ratio was 1.27 months' worth.
Low inventory levels suggest that manufacturers have room to boost production to build stocks.
